questions.question: What are good laboratory practices in toxicological studies? How is it important?
questions.solution_html:
• Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) serve as a standardized quality framework designed to guarantee
  • that laboratory research is dependable, consistent, and honest. By following OECD and national
  • guidelines, GLP mandates that every phase of an experiment—ranging from the ethical treatment of
  • animals to the final reporting of results—is executed with rigorous documentation and uniformity.
  • They major features of GLP are : Strategic Study Design: Ensuring the research logic is sound from
  • the start. Resource Management: Utilizing skilled staff, verified techniques, and precisely tuned
  • equipment. Data Integrity: Maintaining exhaustive and precise records of all activities. Adhering to
  • these standards does more than just a lab's scientific reputation; it is a mandatory prerequisite for
  • regulatory bodies when evaluating chemical safety or approving new drugs. Furthermore, GLP
  • compliance facilitates the international exchange of data, preventing the need for redundant testing
  • across different countries. (2m - practices; 1m -importance)

questions.question: What is the role of Phase I reactions in xenobiotic metabolism?
questions.solution_html:
• Phase I reactions, primarily catalyzed by cytochrome P450 enzymes, serve as the initial step in
  • xenobiotic metabolism by oxidizing, reducing, or hydrolyzing foreign compounds. Their main role is
  • to convert lipophilic xenobiotics into more polar, water-soluble metabolites by introducing or
  • exposing functional groups (e.g., OH, NH2, SH, COOH)
  • Phase I reactions introduce or expose functional groups and make compounds more chemically
  • reactive and slightly more polar.

questions.question: What is LD50 ?
questions.solution_html:
• LD50 (Lethal Dose 50%) is a standard measure of acute toxicity, representing the amount of a
  • substance—administered all at once—required to kill 50% of a test population (usually mice or rats).
  • A lower LD50 indicates higher toxicity. It is typically expressed in milligrams per kilogram of body
  • weight.

questions.question: How xenobiotics redistributed in the body?
questions.solution_html:
• Redistribution of xenobiotics refers to the movement of xenobiotics from one tissue to another after
  • their initial distribution. This process occurs due to changes in blood flow, tissue affinity, and
  • chemical nature of the xenobiotic. Initially, xenobiotics are delivered to highly perfused organs such
  • as the brain, liver, lungs, and kidneys. Over time, xenobiotics may move to less perfused tissues such
  • as adipose tissue, muscle, and bone, where they can be stored. Lipid-soluble xenobiotics show greater
  • redistribution because of their affinity for fat tissues. Examples include DDT, PCBs, and dioxins
  • which accumulate in adipose tissue and are slowly released, causing prolonged and chronic toxic
  • effects.(4/5 relevant points)

questions.question: Differeniate flammable and corrosive chemicals with suitable examples
questions.solution_html:
• Flammable and corrosive chemicals represent two distinct categories of hazardous materials defined
  • by how they interact with their environment and human tissue. Flammable chemicals pose a fire
  • hazard by igniting easily, whereas corrosive chemicals cause damage by chemically destroying
  • living tissues or materials upon contact.
  • Flammable Chemicals: These substances catch fire easily when exposed to air, heat, or a spark.
  • They are classified based on their "flash point"—the lowest temperature at which they produce
  • enough vapor to ignite. Examples: Gasoline, Acetone, Ethanol (Alcohol), Benzene, Butane, Paint
  • Thinners, Kerosene, Sodium, and Potassium.
  • Corrosive Chemicals: These substances cause immediate, severe damage upon contact with living
  • tissue (eyes, skin) or destroy metals. They can cause burns, lesions, and permanent tissue
  • damage. Examples: Hydrochloric Acid Sulfuric Acid , Sodium Hydroxide , Hydrofluoric Acid
  • Bromine, and Ammonia.(Definition of two - 2m, examples for both - 1m)
questions.final_answer: Bromine, and Ammonia.(Definition of two - 2m, examples for both - 1m)

questions.question: How do Agricultural pesticides cause mass mortality in birds?
questions.solution_html:
•  Ingestion of Treated Seeds & Insects: Neonicotinoid pesticides, often coated on seeds, are
  • highly toxic. Birds eating these seeds or insects that have consumed the pesticides are directly
  • poisoned.
  •  Acute Toxicity and Neurological Damage: Pesticides act as neurotoxins, attacking the central
  • nervous system. This causes immediate mortality or debilitating symptoms like loss of
  • coordination and inability to fly.
  •  Starvation and Anorexia: Some pesticides, such as imidacloprid, induce severe anorexia in
  • migrating birds, causing them to lose significant body weight and fat stores, making them unable
  • to complete migration.
  •  Food Source Depletion: Pesticides kill the insects (caterpillars, beetles, flies) that birds rely on to
  • feed their nestlings. The loss of prey, particularly for aerial insectivores (swallows, swifts), causes
  • mass starvation of chicks.
  •  Reproductive Failure: Contamination affects eggshell quality, reduces breeding success, and
  • impairs parental care, leading to reduced offspring survival.
  •  Systemic Exposure: Systemic insecticides are absorbed into all plant tissues, including nectar
  • pollen, and fruit, exposing birds that do not directly eat insects or seeds. (any 4 points)
questions.final_answer: pollen, and fruit, exposing birds that do not directly eat insects or seeds. (any 4 points)

questions.question: How does lipid solubility influence absorption of Xenobiotics?
questions.solution_html:
• Lipid solubility plays a crucial role in the absorption of xenobiotics because biological membranes
  • are composed of a phospholipid bilayer. Xenobiotics that are highly lipid-soluble can easily dissolve
  • in this membrane and pass through it by passive diffusion, without requiring energy or transport
  • proteins. As a result, they are absorbed more rapidly and efficiently compared to water-soluble
  • substances, which cannot easily penetrate the lipid-rich membrane and therefore show slower
  • absorption.(relevant 3/4 points)

questions.question: Compare byssinosis and bagassosis.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare byssinosis and bagassosis.

  • "Monday fever" symptoms. Bagassosis is caused by breathing in moldy sugarcane waste (bagasse)
  • leading to hypersensitivity pneumonitis. (2½m for each definition and differences)

questions.question: Explain sources and bioaccumulation of Mercury. Comment on its acute and chronic / toxicity.
questions.solution_html:
• toxicity.
  • Mercury poisoning primarily results from consuming fish containing high levels of methylmercury
  • inhaling vapor from elemental mercury in broken devices (thermometers/switches), or using
  • contaminated skin-lightening creams. Major environmental sources include coal combustion, small
  • scale gold mining, and industrial pollution.
  • Key sources of mercury exposure include
  •  Contaminated Seafood (Methylmercury): High-mercury fish include shark, swordfish, king
  • mackerel, tuna (especially albacore), orange roughy, marlin, and tilefish.
  •  Industrial and Environmental Pollution: Coal-burning power plants and industrial waste release
  • mercury into the air, which settles into water and enters the food chain.
  •  Broken Products (Elemental Mercury Vapor): Thermometers, barometers, thermostats, and
  • older fluorescent light bulbs contain elemental mercury.
  •  Dental Amalgam Fillings: Older "silver" fillings contain ~50% mercury by weight.
  •  Gold Mining: Small-scale, industrial, and artisanal gold mining often uses mercury to extract
  • gold, leading to severe local exposure and environmental contamination.
  •  Consumer Products: Certain skin-lightening creams, soaps, and traditional medicines may
  • contain mercury.
  • Those at higher risk include pregnant women, nursing mothers, young children, and people with high
  • consumption of predatory fish. (2½m for sources and bioaccumulation, 2½m for toxicity)
questions.final_answer: consumption of predatory fish. (2½m for sources and bioaccumulation, 2½m for toxicity)

questions.question: Define occupational cancer and write a short note on the major occupational cancers.
questions.solution_html:
• Definition – The type of cancer which arises from long-term exposure to workplace carcinogens like
  • smoke, various chemicals, solar radiation etc. ((1 mark))
  • Major occupational cancers – skin cancer, lung cancer, bladder cancer, leukemia
  • Skin Cancer: Skin cancer involves uncontrolled growth of abnormal skin cells, typically due to
  • ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or artificial sources. The major types are basal cell carcinoma
  • squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma. Early signs include changes in existing moles, shiny bumps
  • rough scaly patches or lesions that itch or bleed. Preventive strategies include UV protection
  • protective clothing and minimizing exposure to known carcinogens.
  • Lung Cancer: Lung cancer develops when abnormal cells in the lungs multiply uncontrollably
  • forming tumors that destroy healthy tissue. While smoking is the leading cause, occupational
  • exposure to carcinogens such as asbestos, radiation and second-hand smoke also increases risk. Early
  • symptoms are often absent. Advanced disease presents with persistent cough, chest pain, hemoptysis
  • breathlessness, hoarseness, weight loss and fatigue. Lung cancers are categorized as: Non-small cell
  • lung cancer (NSCLC) and Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
  • Bladder Cancer: Bladder cancer begins in the urothelial lining of the bladder, where uncontrolled cell
  • growth forms tumors. Early symptoms include hematuria, frequent urination, urgency and painful
  • urination. Occupational exposure is a major contributor, particularly to aromatic amines found in the
  • dye, rubber, chemical and paint industries Hairdressers, barbers and firefighters also face increased
  • risk through chronic exposure to carcinogens. Types include - Urothelial carcinoma, Squamous cell
  • carcinoma , Adenocarcinoma , Small cell carcinoma
  • Leukaemia: Leukaemia is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow involving uncontrolled growth of
  • abnormal white blood cells. These cells fail to function properly, accumulate in the bone marrow and
  • suppress normal blood cell production, leading to anemia, infection and bleeding tendencies.
  • Risk factors include ionizing radiation, benzene exposure and certain chemotherapeutic agents
  • (alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil). Workers involved in chemical
  • pharmaceutical, paint, plastic and oil industries may be increased risk due to benzene exposure.
  • Occupational exposure to cytotoxic drugs dur preparation or administration also poses hazards to
  • healthcare workers. Symptoms include easy bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, frequent infection
  • fatigue and pallor. Treatment varies by leukemia type, with chemotherapy remaining mainstay.
  • (Explanation on the types – (1 mark) each for 2-3 relevant points)
questions.final_answer: (Explanation on the types – each for 2-3 relevant points)

questions.question: What are good laboratory practices in toxicological studies? How is it important?
questions.solution_html:
• Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) serve as a standardized quality framework designed to guarantee
  • that laboratory research is dependable, consistent, and honest. By following OECD and national
  • guidelines, GLP mandates that every phase of an experiment—ranging from the ethical treatment of
  • animals to the final reporting of results—is executed with rigorous documentation and uniformity.
  • They major features of GLP are : Strategic Study Design: Ensuring the research logic is sound from
  • the start. Resource Management: Utilizing skilled staff, verified techniques, and precisely tuned
  • equipment. Data Integrity: Maintaining exhaustive and precise records of all activities. Adhering to
  • these standards does more than just a lab's scientific reputation; it is a mandatory prerequisite for
  • regulatory bodies when evaluating chemical safety or approving new drugs. Furthermore, GLP
  • compliance facilitates the international exchange of data, preventing the need for redundant testing
  • across different countries. (2m - practices; 1m -importance)

  • exposing functional groups (e.g., OH, NH2, SH, COOH)
  • Phase I reactions introduce or expose functional groups and make compounds more chemically
  • reactive and slightly more polar.

questions.question: How xenobiotics redistributed in the body?
questions.solution_html:
• Redistribution of xenobiotics refers to the movement of xenobiotics from one tissue to another after
  • their initial distribution. This process occurs due to changes in blood flow, tissue affinity, and
  • chemical nature of the xenobiotic. Initially, xenobiotics are delivered to highly perfused organs such
  • as the brain, liver, lungs, and kidneys. Over time, xenobiotics may move to less perfused tissues such
  • as adipose tissue, muscle, and bone, where they can be stored. Lipid-soluble xenobiotics show greater
  • redistribution because of their affinity for fat tissues. Examples include DDT, PCBs, and dioxins
  • which accumulate in adipose tissue and are slowly released, causing prolonged and chronic toxic
  • effects.(4/5 relevant points)

questions.question: How do Agricultural pesticides cause mass mortality in birds?
questions.solution_html:
•  Ingestion of Treated Seeds & Insects: Neonicotinoid pesticides, often coated on seeds, are
  • highly toxic. Birds eating these seeds or insects that have consumed the pesticides are directly
  • poisoned.
  •  Acute Toxicity and Neurological Damage: Pesticides act as neurotoxins, attacking the central
  • nervous system. This causes immediate mortality or debilitating symptoms like loss of
  • coordination and inability to fly.
  •  Starvation and Anorexia: Some pesticides, such as imidacloprid, induce severe anorexia in
  • migrating birds, causing them to lose significant body weight and fat stores, making them unable
  • to complete migration.
  •  Food Source Depletion: Pesticides kill the insects (caterpillars, beetles, flies) that birds rely on to
  • feed their nestlings. The loss of prey, particularly for aerial insectivores (swallows, swifts), causes
  • mass starvation of chicks.
  •  Reproductive Failure: Contamination affects eggshell quality, reduces breeding success, and
  • impairs parental care, leading to reduced offspring survival.
  •  Systemic Exposure: Systemic insecticides are absorbed into all plant tissues, including nectar
  • pollen, and fruit, exposing birds that do not directly eat insects or seeds. (any 4 points)
questions.final_answer: pollen, and fruit, exposing birds that do not directly eat insects or seeds. (any 4 points)

questions.question: Define occupational cancer and write a short note on the major occupational cancers.
questions.solution_html:
• Definition – The type of cancer which arises from long-term exposure to workplace carcinogens like
  • smoke, various chemicals, solar radiation etc. ((1 mark))
  • Major occupational cancers – skin cancer, lung cancer, bladder cancer, leukemia
  • Skin Cancer: Skin cancer involves uncontrolled growth of abnormal skin cells, typically due to
  • ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or artificial sources. The major types are basal cell carcinoma
  • squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma. Early signs include changes in existing moles, shiny bumps
  • rough scaly patches or lesions that itch or bleed. Preventive strategies include UV protection
  • protective clothing and minimizing exposure to known carcinogens.
  • Lung Cancer: Lung cancer develops when abnormal cells in the lungs multiply uncontrollably
  • forming tumors that destroy healthy tissue. While smoking is the leading cause, occupational
  • exposure to carcinogens such as asbestos, radiation and second-hand smoke also increases risk. Early
  • symptoms are often absent. Advanced disease presents with persistent cough, chest pain, hemoptysis
  • breathlessness, hoarseness, weight loss and fatigue. Lung cancers are categorized as: Non-small cell
  • lung cancer (NSCLC) and Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
  • Bladder Cancer: Bladder cancer begins in the urothelial lining of the bladder, where uncontrolled cell
  • growth forms tumors. Early symptoms include hematuria, frequent urination, urgency and painful
  • urination. Occupational exposure is a major contributor, particularly to aromatic amines found in the
  • dye, rubber, chemical and paint industries Hairdressers, barbers and firefighters also face increased
  • risk through chronic exposure to carcinogens. Types include - Urothelial carcinoma, Squamous cell
  • carcinoma , Adenocarcinoma , Small cell carcinoma
  • Leukaemia: Leukaemia is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow involving uncontrolled growth of
  • abnormal white blood cells. These cells fail to function properly, accumulate in the bone marrow and
  • suppress normal blood cell production, leading to anemia, infection and bleeding tendencies.
  • Risk factors include ionizing radiation, benzene exposure and certain chemotherapeutic agents
  • (alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil). Workers involved in chemical
  • pharmaceutical, paint, plastic and oil industries may be increased risk due to benzene exposure.
  • Occupational exposure to cytotoxic drugs dur preparation or administration also poses hazards to
  • healthcare workers. Symptoms include easy bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, frequent infection
  • fatigue and pallor. Treatment varies by leukemia type, with chemotherapy remaining mainstay.
  • (Explanation on the types – (1 mark) each for 2-3 relevant points)
questions.final_answer: (Explanation on the types – each for 2-3 relevant points)
